units.spoken: Training DDPG: Target Networks, Replay and Noise
Three fixes that make Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) learn to control a robot arm.

Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) has three faults. Its critic learns from targets that move with every update. It learns from back-to-back steps that look alike. And its actor repeats one motion and never tries anything new. Left alone, these faults can make the arm's learning blow up or stall. This page teaches three fixes that keep it training.

The agent is the learner that picks the moves. A state is the agent's situation right now. A move, or action, is one choice the agent can make in a state. A reward is the number the world hands back after each move, good or bad.

The running example is the Reacher task: a robot arm with two joints whose actions are four torques. A torque is a turning force a motor applies at a joint. On the Reacher each torque is a number from -1 to 1. Each joint can turn about two axes, so each joint gets two torques. Every step the arm senses its state, 33 numbers describing the position, rotation and speed of its parts, and earns a small reward of plus 0.1 per step whenever its hand is inside a moving goal. The repo that trains the Reacher arms on this page, RF-DDPG, trains 20 such arms side by side.

Take a look at this figure. Two joints, a shoulder and an elbow, each turning about two axes, so four torques turn the arm. The hand sits near a dashed goal circle that moves. The lesson is the task: read the pose and speed, send four torques, and earn a small reward when the hand is inside the goal.

Figure 1 shows the Reacher arm this page trains: a shoulder joint and an elbow joint, each turning about two axes, so the arm takes four torques. The hand sits near a dashed goal circle that moves. Take one step: the arm reads its pose and speed, sends four torques, and earns a small reward when its hand is inside the goal.

The return is all the reward still to come, with later rewards counted a little less. A move's value Q of s and a, also called its score, is the return the agent expects if it makes move a in state s and plays on from there.
DDPG learns two networks for the arm.

The deterministic actor mu sub thay-ta is a network with weights thay-ta that outputs one action every time, with no random draw. The critic Q sub fee is a network with weights fee that scores a state and an action together; its score stands for the return the agent expects.
The actor proposes the arm's torques, and the critic tells it which way to change them to score higher.

sections.section: 1 The fixes that keep DDPG training stable

units.spoken: Section one, The fixes that keep DDPG training stable
1.1 Copies that change slowly
Slow copies hold the target still
What. Picture a target that shifts with every update. The critic's target is built from its own scores, so it moves as the critic moves.
How. Each slow copy takes only a small share of its live weights per update.
Why. When it works, the target barely moves, and the critic's scores settle.
The critic learns by being pulled toward a target, the step's reward plus its own score for what comes next, counted a little less.
The Deep Q-Network (DQN) method scores moves with one network, its Q-network. DQN had the same problem of a target that moves, and fixed it with a second network.

DQN is a value method: it learns by scoring moves. DDPG is an actor-critic method: its critic scores moves and its actor picks the torques. DQN keeps a target network, a second copy with weights fee prime that computes the targets, and refreshes it all at once every 10000 steps, a hard copy. In DDPG the critic plays the Q-network's part, and there the slow copy is updated only a little at a time.

In DDPG both the actor and the critic have a slow copy, and the targets are built from those copies. The discount gamma sets how much a reward one step later still counts. The DDPG critic's target is the step's reward plus the discounted score the slow critic gives to the slow actor's next torques.
On the arm, each slow copy must still follow the network it copies, or the critic would learn from stale scores.

The live networks are the actor and critic being trained, with weights thay-ta and fee. The soft update blends a small share of the live weights into each slow copy after every update, instead of overwriting it.
Equation 1. The Reacher arm's critic learns from a target built out of its own scores, so a target that moves with every update would chase itself, and the arm's scores would never settle.
Take a look at this equation. The slow copies creep toward the live networks a small share at a time, so the targets the critic learns from barely move.

The first line, the slow critic. Fee prime is the slow critic's weights, the copy that builds the critic's targets. The arrow replaces the left side with the right side. Tau times fee is a small share of the live critic's weights: tau is the share blended per update. The plus adds one minus tau times fee prime, the rest of the slow copy's own. Fee prime gets replaced by tau times fee plus one minus tau times fee prime. One minus tau is what stays, so the two shares add to one, a weighted average. With tau small, each slow weight moves only a hair per update, while DQN's hard copy blends in all of the live weights at once. Intuitively, the slow copy creeps toward the live network instead of jumping to it.
Intuition. The target the critic learns from must hold still while the critic moves, so the slow copy creeps toward the live network instead of jumping to it.
Example. Picture the target the critic learns from next: it barely moves after one update, because the slow copy behind it barely moved.

The second line, the slow actor. Thay-ta prime is the slow actor's weights, the copy whose next torques the slow critic scores. The blend takes tau times thay-ta, a small share of the live actor's weights, plus one minus tau times thay-ta prime, the rest of its own. Tau is the same share, so the actor's copy trails at the same slow pace. Both slow copies sit inside the critic's target, the step's reward plus the slow score of the slow actor's next torques, so after each update the targets move slowly instead of chasing the live networks. Intuitively, the slow actor trails the same way as the slow critic, so the torques the target scores stay close to the ones it scored before.
Intuition. The slow actor trails the same way as the slow critic, so the torques the target scores stay close to the ones it scored before.
Example. Picture the slow actor's next torques: they barely change after one update, because the slow actor behind them barely moved.
So both slow copies blend a small share of their live networks after each update, and the targets move slowly instead of chasing the live networks.
A hard copy overwrites the slow copy with the live weights every 10000 steps.

Raising the share makes the slow copies follow the live networks faster, and the target wobbles more; lowering it holds the target still but slows learning. At the extremes, a share of 1 copies the live weights at once, and a share of 0 freezes the slow copies.
The code below blends a small share of the live weights into each slow copy.

This code blends a small share of the live weights into each slow copy. A function pairs each slow weight with its live weight and blends a small share in, and it runs once for the critic pair and once for the actor pair. The share is TAU, 1e-3, the target update share. The lesson is the blend: a small share per update, so the slow copies creep toward the live networks.
1. Pairs each slow weight with its live weight and loops over the pairs.
2. Blends a small share of each live weight into its slow copy, once for the critic pair and once for the actor pair. TAU is 1e-3, the target update share.
1.2 A replay buffer of past steps
A memory of past steps, sampled at random
What. Picture revising only the last page read. Back-to-back steps look alike, so the network fits the last few and forgets the rest.
How. Training draws a random batch from a large memory of past steps, mixing old and new.
Why. When it works, each batch looks like the whole run.
Learning from stored past steps is called off-policy, and learning without a model of the arm is called model-free: DDPG is both.
The code below stores steps in a memory and draws a random batch from it.

This code stores steps in a memory and draws a random batch from it. It creates a memory that holds 100000 steps, fills it with a thousand stored steps, and draws a random batch of 256. The lesson is the mix: old and new steps together, so each batch looks like the whole run.
1. Creates the memory and fills it with a thousand stored steps. done marks whether the arm's run ended on this step.
2. Draws a random batch from the memory. BUFFER_SIZE is 100000 steps, the memory's size, and BATCH is 256 steps, the batch drawn from it.
1.3 Random nudges with memory
A nudge with memory
What. Picture the arm repeating one motion forever. The actor always names the same torques for the same state, so on its own it never tries anything new.
How. A nudge that keeps most of itself joins the torques and drifts smoothly.
Why. When it works, the arm sweeps smoothly into new motions instead of repeating one move.

Exploration noise is a small random nudge added to the actor's torques while it learns, so the arm tries moves it is not sure about. Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) noise is a nudge with memory: it drifts smoothly instead of jumping from step to step.

Take a look at this figure. The same random kicks are drawn two ways over a stretch of steps. The upper trace draws a fresh kick each step, so it jumps from side to side with no memory. The lower trace keeps most of each nudge, so it drifts smoothly around zero. The lesson is the memory: a nudge that keeps most of itself sweeps the arm smoothly instead of twitching it.

Figure 2 draws the same random kicks two ways over a stretch of steps. The upper trace draws a fresh kick each step, so it jumps from side to side with no memory; the lower trace keeps most of each nudge, so it drifts smoothly around zero. Take one kick that lands far out: on the upper trace the next step forgets it, while on the lower trace it still shapes the nudge several steps later.

Equation 2. A nudge with memory. The Reacher arm needs a nudge that drifts from step to step, so its actor tries new torques instead of repeating one motion: the nudge carries the arm into motions it would never try on its own.
Take a look at this equation. The nudge keeps most of itself from step to step, drifts smoothly, and joins the actor's torques, clipped to what the arm can give.

The first line. X is the current nudge, one number per torque. The arrow replaces the left side with the right side. The right side starts from x and takes away kappa times x, the pull back to zero: each step the nudge keeps one minus kappa of itself. Then it adds sigma sub O U times xi, a fresh kick. Xi is a draw from the standard normal, the bell curve centred at zero, so most draws land near zero. Sigma sub O U is the size of each kick. X gets replaced by x minus kappa times x plus sigma sub O U times xi. Unlike noise drawn fresh each step, this nudge keeps most of itself, so the arm sweeps smoothly instead of twitching. Intuitively, a nudge that remembers most of itself sweeps the arm smoothly.
Intuition. A nudge that forgets the last step would twitch the arm at random; a nudge that remembers most of itself sweeps the arm smoothly.
Example. Take a nudge that has drifted far from zero: the pull drags it back a little each step, so it wanders home instead of staying out.

The second line. A is the four torques the arm is sent. Mu sub thay-ta of s is the actor's torques for the state s, the 33 numbers describing one arm, from the actor network with weights thay-ta. The plus adds x, the nudge, which keeps most of itself, is pulled back toward zero, and takes a fresh kick. A equals mu sub thay-ta of s plus x: the actor's torques, shifted by the nudge. Intuitively, the actor alone repeats itself, so the nudge is added on top to make the arm try something it would not try alone.
Intuition. The actor alone repeats itself, so the nudge is added on top to make the arm try something it would not try alone.
Example. Take the arm at one pose: the actor names its torques, the nudge shifts them a little, and the arm is sent the shifted torques.

The third line. A is the torques, the actor's torques shifted by the nudge. The arrow means the left side is replaced by the right side. Clip keeps each torque inside minus 1 to 1: a torque above 1 becomes 1, a torque below minus 1 becomes minus 1, and one already inside stays as it is, so no torque asks for more than the arm can give. A gets replaced by clip of a, minus 1, 1. The clip acts after the nudge joins, so a torque the nudge pushed past the arm's limit is held at the limit instead of being sent. Intuitively, a torque bigger than the motor can give is a wasted order, so the arm's torques are held inside what it can do.
Intuition. A torque bigger than the motor can give is a wasted order, so the arm's torques are held inside what it can do.
Example. Take a torque the nudge pushed past 1: clip pins it at 1, and the arm is sent a torque it can give.
So the nudge drifts smoothly from step to step, shifts the actor's torques, and clip holds every torque inside what the arm can give.
Here thay-ta always means the actor's weights. The DDPG paper writes the pull as thay-ta, while this page writes it as kappa.

Raising the pull brings each nudge back toward zero faster, so the arm wanders less far; lowering it lets each nudge drift longer. Raising the size of each kick makes the nudges bigger, so the arm tries wider moves; lowering it makes the nudges smaller and the arm stays closer to what it already does. With no kick at all, the arm stops exploring.

Take a look at this figure. The three stabilizers stack up, each with the failure it prevents. Slow copies blend a small share per update so the target barely moves. The replay buffer stores steps in order and trains on random batches so recent steps do not dominate. OU noise smooths the actor's exploration so it does not repeat one move forever. The lesson is the set: each fix steadies one part of training.

Figure 3 stacks the three stabilizers, each with the failure it prevents. The three fixes taught here are called stabilizers because each one steadies training. The DDPG paper names a fourth fix, batch normalization, which steadies the networks' inputs. Slow copies blend a small share of the live weights per update so the target barely moves; the replay buffer stores steps in order and trains on random batches so recent steps do not dominate; OU noise smooths the actor's exploration so it does not repeat one move forever. Take the slow-copy panel: the live critic moves fast while the target critic barely moves.

sections.section: 2 One training update with every fix

units.spoken: Section two, One training update with every fix
One update, six steps
What. Picture one batch of past steps going through the whole loop. The update draws the batch, builds the targets, moves the critic, moves the actor, and blends both slow copies one at a time.
How. One sampled batch drives all six steps in order, each step feeding the next.
Why. When it works, the critic moves closer to its targets while the targets barely move.

Take a look at this figure. One training update runs as a loop. The replay buffer feeds a random batch; the slow actor names the next torques, the slow critic scores them, the reward joins the target, the critic moves toward it, the live actor climbs the landscape, and the slow copies blend a small share. The lesson is the loop: one batch drives every part in order.

Figure 4 shows one training update as a loop. The loop is the point: one batch drives every part in order. The replay buffer feeds a batch; the slow actor names the next torques, the slow critic scores them, the reward joins the target, the critic moves toward it, the live actor climbs the landscape, and copies blend a small share. Take one batch: it pulls the critic toward its targets while the slow copies barely move.

Try the walkthrough. Press Play to run one training update through the six steps, or step through it with Next. Watch the batch feed the target, the critic move toward it, the actor climb, and the slow copies blend a small share. The equation card opens at the last two steps, step 5 for the slow critic and step 6 for the slow actor. Press Reset to start the walk again.
The Reacher arm's slow copies trail the live networks by a small share each update, so the targets the critic learns from barely move.
Take a look at this equation. The slow copies trail the live networks by a small share each update, so the targets barely move.

The first line, the slow critic. Fee prime is the slow critic's weights, the copy that builds the critic's targets, and the prime marks the slow copy. The blend takes tau times fee, a small share of the live critic's weights, plus one minus tau times fee prime, the rest of the slow copy's own. With tau small, each slow weight moves a hair, so the targets the next update learns from barely change. Intuitively, without blending a small share, the slow copy would jump to the live weights each update, and the target would jump with it, so the critic would chase a moving mark.

Intuition. Without blending a small share, the slow copy would jump to the live weights each update, and the target would jump with it, so the critic would chase a moving mark. Blending a small share keeps the target almost still while the live critic learns.
Example. One slow critic weight moves only a hair in this update, so the targets the next update learns from barely change.

The second line, the slow actor. Thay-ta prime is the slow actor's weights, the copy whose next torques the slow critic scores, and the prime marks the slow copy. The blend takes tau times thay-ta, a small share of the live actor's weights, plus one minus tau times thay-ta prime, the rest of its own. Tau is the same share, so the actor's copy trails at the same slow pace. After each update, both slow copies drift a small share toward their live networks, and the targets move slowly instead of chasing them. Intuitively, the slow actor trails the same way as the slow critic, so the torques the target scores stay close to the ones it scored before.
Intuition. The slow actor trails the same way as the slow critic, so the torques the target scores stay close to the ones it scored before, and the target does not jump when the actor moves.
Example. One slow actor weight moves only a hair in this update, so the slow actor's next torques barely change.
So both slow copies blend a small share after each update, and the targets barely move while the live networks learn.

The soft-update card opens only at the last two steps, step 5 for the slow critic and step 6 for the slow actor, because only those steps blend the slow copies: each slow weight takes a small share tau of its live weight plus the rest of its own. The first four steps are 1 draw a random batch, 2 build the target, 3 move the critic, and 4 move the actor.
An episode is one run from the start until it ends. The code marks where each arm's episode ended, so no future score is added past it.

The code below runs one training update on a sampled batch, in six steps. The target block is step 2, the critic block is step 3, the actor block is step 4, and the last block holds steps 5 and 6. Step 1, drawing the batch, is the sampling line in the replay code.
First, the target for each step comes from the slow copies.

This code builds each step's target from the slow copies. It asks the slow actor for the next torques and the slow critic for their score, then returns the reward plus the discounted slow score, with nothing added where an episode ended. The discount is GAMMA, 0.99, and the clip norm is CLIP, 1. The lesson is the target: built from slow copies, so it barely moves.

1. Builds each step's target from the slow copies; done marks the end of an episode, so the target adds no future value there (the DDPG critic's target, on the DDPG page). GAMMA is 0.99, the discount, and CLIP is 1, the critic clip norm.
Next, the critic moves toward those targets.

This code moves the critic toward its targets. It builds the targets, scores the stored torques, and pulls the scores toward the targets by mean squared error, capping the step and stepping the optimizer. The lesson is the pull: shrinking the gap between scores and targets.

1. Moves the critic toward those targets: mse_loss is the mean squared error, the average of the squared gaps between the critic's scores q and the targets y, so shrinking it pulls the scores toward the targets (the DDPG critic's loss, on the DDPG page). The clip caps the size of each critic step: raising it lets steps grow larger, lowering it steadies learning, and a huge value turns the cap off. critic_opt is the Adam optimizer for the critic, at a learning rate of 1e-3. Adam adapts each weight's step size using its past gradients.
Then the actor moves so its torques shift the way the critic's score rises.

This code moves the actor so its torques shift the way the critic's score rises. It scores the actor's torques with the critic and sets the actor's loss to minus that score, so raising the score lowers the loss. The lesson is the trick: the actor climbs by making the critic's score bigger.
1. Moves the actor so its torques shift the way the critic's score rises (the DDPG actor update, on the DDPG page). actor_opt is the Adam optimizer for the actor, at a learning rate of 1e-3.
Last, both slow copies blend a small step toward the live networks.

This code blends both slow copies a small step toward the live networks. It runs the soft update once for the actor pair and once for the critic pair. The lesson is the catch-up: a small share per update, so the targets barely move.

sections.section: 3 Switching off the slow copies in a live toy DDPG

units.spoken: Section three, Switching off the slow copies in a live toy DDPG
Slow copies on versus off
What. Picture the same toy arm learning twice, once with slow copies and once without. Without them the critic chases its own live scores, so its scores run away.
How. A switch turns the slow copies on or off for the same arm.
Why. When it works, the arm stays on its goal with the copies on, and swings wide without them.
The curve shows how close the arm stays to the goal, checked after each episode with the nudges switched off.

Here every reward is a cost, a negative number for being far from the goal and for moving hard, not the Reacher's small number for being inside the goal. The critic starts at zero, so it is too hopeful at first, and its scores fall as it learns the costs.

Take a look at this figure. A one-joint arm learns to follow a wandering goal, with the slow copies on. The arm panel shows the hand on the goal ring, the closeness curve stays near the top across the run, and the critic's line drifts slowly below the most any step can earn. The lesson is the slow drift: the targets barely move, so the critic learns from a steady mark.

Figure 5 shows the toy arm learning with the slow copies on: the arm follows its wandering goal while the critic's expectations drift slowly. That slow drift is the point: the targets barely move, so the critic learns from a steady mark. The arm panel shows the hand on the goal ring; the closeness curve stays near the top across the run; the critic's line drifts slowly below the most any step can earn. Take one episode: the arm stays on its goal while the critic's line moves only a little.

Try the toy. Flip the switch to turn the slow copies on or off for the same arm, then press Play to run the episodes. Watch the arm follow its wandering goal, the closeness curve across the run, and the critic's line against the most any step can earn. Each run plays its episodes, then stops, and scores past the edge are pinned there. The lesson is the contrast: with the copies on the arm stays on its goal, and with them off the critic's scores run away.

Take a look at this figure. The same run with the slow copies off: the critic chases its own live scores, so the run falls apart early. The closeness curve plunges after the first episode and stops, and the critic's line is pinned at the top edge, past the most any step can earn. The score after the second episode reaches 262,221,285. The lesson is the failure: without slow copies the scores run away and the run stops early.

Figure 6 shows the same run with the slow copies off: the critic chases its own live scores, so the run falls apart early. The closeness curve plunges after the first episode and stops; the critic's line is pinned at the top edge, past the most any step can earn.

sections.section: 4 Training on the Reacher with many arms

units.spoken: Section four, Training on the Reacher with many arms

The update runs in bursts while the arms keep acting. The replay buffer dominates memory; the four networks are small next to it. The same three fixes ship in Stable-Baselines3, a widely used reinforcement learning code library.
4.1 DDPG solving the many-arm Reacher
The run trains 20 arms, and evaluates with the noise switched off. Evaluation means testing the trained actor with exploration switched off.

Take a look at this figure. The per-episode mean score over the 20 arms, plotted against episode. The horizontal axis counts episodes and the vertical axis counts score. Marker 1 is where the mean first reaches the solve bar, around episode 92, and marker 2 is the final episode, where the trailing 100-episode mean reaches 30.3. The lesson is the solve: the run counts as solved when the mean reaches 30 averaged over 100 consecutive episodes.

Figure 7 plots the per-episode mean score over the 20 arms against episode, from the repo's own run. A run counts as solved when the mean score reaches 30 averaged over 100 consecutive episodes. The plotted mean first reaches 30 around episode 92, dips to 27.1 around episode 107, and stays above 30 only from episode 109 to 161, 53 episodes. The trailing 100-episode mean is the average over the most recent 100 episodes. The plotted line is the raw per-episode mean and the marker is the trailing mean, which reaches 30.3 at episode 161, so the run is solved at its end.

sections.section: 5 When each stabilizer matters and how training fails

units.spoken: Section five, When each stabilizer matters and how training fails

Take a look at this table. It says when each stabilizer matters most. Slow copies matter when the critic's target is built from its own fast-changing scores: soft updates hold the target values almost still, which steadies training. Replay matters when consecutive steps look alike, as with many arms moving smoothly, and a smaller memory adapts faster when the task changes. Exploration noise matters early, when the actor has never seen the goal region: turn it down as the arm improves and switch it off at evaluation. The rows compare by timing: slow copies steady the target all through training, replay fixes the batches, and noise matters most at the start.
DQN's target takes a max, the highest of the scores its Q-network gives the next moves.

Overestimation means the values climb above the return the agent really earns, because a max over noisy guesses picks lucky ones. (Double DQN, which picks with the live network and scores with its target network) In DDPG the actor plays the role of the max, because it learns to pick the torques the critic scores highest.

The first failure below has a named fix: Twin Delayed DDPG (TD3), a method that builds on DDPG. It changes three things: two critics instead of one, smoothed target torques, and a slower actor update. Each item in the list names the failure, why it bites, and the fix, with why the fix works.

The critic's scores climb too high. The actor picks the torques the critic scores highest, so the scores climb above the return the arm really earns. TD3 fixes it: a second critic checks the first, so a single lucky guess cannot set the target on its own.

The slow copies move too fast. When the blend share is too big, the target wobbles with every update and the critic's scores chase their own changes. Keep the blend share tau small: a small share blended in per update leaves the target almost still, so the critic learns from a steady mark.

Too little exploration. The actor always names the same torques for the same state, so the arm repeats one motion and never finds the goal. Raise the OU kick size: bigger kicks carry the arm into new motions, so it tries torques it would never try on its own.

Noise left on at evaluation. The noise keeps shaking the torques at test time, so the arm wobbles and its score drops. Switch the noise off at evaluation: with no nudge added, the arm is sent exactly the torques the trained actor names, so its score shows what it really learned.

The critic's gradients are not zeroed before its step. Each step adds the last step's gradients to the new ones, so the critic's step mixes stale gradients in and the critic drifts. Zero the critic's gradients before its step: each step then learns only from its own batch, so the critic moves only where the current targets pull it.

A torque leaves the -1 to 1 range. The arm is asked for a torque its motor cannot give. Clip each torque into -1 to 1 after adding noise: a torque past the limit is held at the limit, so the arm is always sent a torque it can give.

The future value is added past the end of an episode. The target counts reward after the run ended, so the critic learns from reward that never happened. Zero the future value at the end of an episode: with done marking the end, the target is just the step's reward, so no reward past the end leaks in.
Section six, Methods that build on DDPG

Twin Delayed DDPG (TD3) builds on DDPG with three changes. It keeps two critics and trusts the lower score, so a lucky high guess cannot lift the target. It adds a small clipped nudge to the target torques, called target policy smoothing, so a narrow spike in the critic's score cannot be exploited. It updates the actor less often than the critic, so the actor moves only once the critic's scores have settled. Use it when the critic's scores climb too high.

Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) changes the actor: instead of one set of torques per state, it learns a range of torques, a spread of moves, and earns a bonus for keeping that spread wide. Wide means the arm still tries different torques in the same state instead of settling on one. Use it when the arm settles too early on one motion.

Multi-agent DDPG trains several arms or players at once. Each agent keeps its own actor, but each agent's critic sees all the agents, so it judges one arm's move in the light of what the others do. Use it when several agents learn together and one arm's reward depends on the others.
Each of them still learns from a replay memory of past steps, and each one builds on the off-policy actor-critic update with target networks.
